(CNN) -- A mother and her infant were killed by a tornado that hit Murfreesboro, Tennessee, on Friday, a family member told CNN. Powerful tornado winds ripped through Murfreesboro, Tennessee, Friday, leaving a trail of destruction. About 36 people were injured, at least two of them critically, officials said. Early Saturday, officials said  about 250 homes had been damaged or destroyed. The woman who was killed, Kori Bryant, was at home with her daughter, Olivia, when the tornado struck, said family member Mark McClure. Another family member, who found the mother and daughter after the tornado, said attempts were made to resuscitate the infant, but she couldn't be saved, according to McClure. The baby was found in her car seat. Her parents had put her in the seat, thinking it would be safer for her, McClure said. The Bryants were in the hallway with the baby when the tornado struck. The woman's husband, John Bryant, was found about two houses away, McClure said. His back and ribs were broken, and a lung had collapsed. He was taken to Vanderbilt University Hospital, and he will undergo surgery when his blood pressure stabilizes, McClure said. John's brother told him yesterday that his wife and daughter had died, McClure said. The bad weather began about noon when a band of severe thunderstorms swept across the state from the southwest, said Donnie Smith, a public information officer with the Tennessee Department of Emergency Management in Nashville. Just before 1:40 p.m., the tornado hit Murfreesboro in Rutherford County, 30 miles southeast of Nashville, he said. Thirty-six people were treated for tornado-related injuries at Middle Tennessee Medical Center in Murfreesboro, said hospital spokeswoman Martha Tolbert. The search-and-rescue effort was continuing into the evening, Smith said.  Watch damage caused by tornado in Murfreesboro » . Elsewhere in the region, the town of Mena, Arkansas, is cleaning up after a tornado roared through, killing three people and damaging or destroying more than 100 homes, an Arkansas official said. The town looked like a "war zone" as soldiers from the Arkansas National Guard went house to house searching for victims of the twister that hit Thursday night, said Capt. Christopher Heathscott. About 50 soldiers also helped with security and food distribution. Mena, population 6,000, took a heavy hit on the west side of town, as the storm swept through downtown before heading up state Highway 71, said Tommy Jackson from the state Department of Emergency Management. "It looks like a war zone out here," said James Reeves, also from the department.  Watch scenes of devastation in Mena » . The tornado damaged the county hospital, Mena City Hall, a middle school, churches, a library, the Masonic lodge and the courthouse -- which houses the 911 emergency dispatch center and a detention center, Reeves said. He said electricity and gas were out in the western half of the city. Two plants at an industrial park were destroyed, said reporter Charles Crowson of CNN affiliate KTHV-TV. He said utility crews were trying to stop a gas leak there. Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd told Crowson the county detention center was "uninhabitable." There were 18 inmates in the jail at the time of the tornado, and they were moved to neighboring jurisdictions, he said. iReport.com: Are you there? Send photos, video . CNN's Melissa Roberts and Dave Alsup contributed to this report.

outputs.L2:
(CNN) — A tornado that struck Murfreesboro, Tennessee, on Friday killed a woman and her baby, according to one of their relatives. The powerful storm tore through the city, causing widespread destruction. Officials reported roughly 36 injuries, including at least two people in critical condition. By early Saturday, authorities estimated that approximately 250 houses had been damaged or completely destroyed.

Relative Mark McClure identified the victims as Kori Bryant and her daughter, Olivia, who were inside their home when the tornado arrived. McClure said another relative discovered them afterward and tried to revive the infant, but the effort was unsuccessful.

Olivia was found secured in her car seat. Her parents had placed her there because they believed it would provide greater protection, McClure said. The Bryant family was sheltering in a hallway with the baby when the tornado hit.

Kori’s husband, John Bryant, was located about two homes away. He suffered fractures to his back and ribs, as well as a collapsed lung, McClure said. John was transported to Vanderbilt University Hospital and was expected to have surgery once his blood pressure became stable. McClure added that John’s brother informed him the previous day that his wife and daughter had been killed.

The severe weather began around noon, when a line of intense thunderstorms moved across Tennessee from the southwest, according to Donnie Smith, a public information officer for the Tennessee Department of Emergency Management in Nashville. Smith said the tornado reached Murfreesboro, in Rutherford County about 30 miles southeast of Nashville, shortly before 1:40 p.m.

Middle Tennessee Medical Center in Murfreesboro treated 36 people for storm-related injuries, hospital spokeswoman Martha Tolbert said. Search-and-rescue operations continued into the evening, according to Smith.

Video showed the destruction left by the Murfreesboro tornado.

In Arkansas, residents of Mena were also clearing debris after a tornado swept through the town Thursday night. The storm killed three people and damaged or demolished more than 100 homes, an Arkansas official said.

Capt. Christopher Heathscott described Mena as resembling a “war zone” while Arkansas National Guard troops searched homes one by one for victims. Approximately 50 soldiers also assisted with security and the distribution of food.

Mena, a community of 6,000 residents, sustained particularly serious damage on its western side. The tornado passed through the downtown area before continuing along state Highway 71, said Tommy Jackson of the Arkansas Department of Emergency Management.

“It looks like a war zone out here,” said James Reeves, another department representative.

Footage documented the devastation in Mena.

Reeves said the tornado damaged numerous buildings, including the county hospital, Mena City Hall, a middle school, several churches, a library, the Masonic lodge and the courthouse. The courthouse contained both the 911 dispatch center and a detention facility. Electricity and gas service were unavailable throughout the city’s western half, he added.

Charles Crowson, a reporter for CNN affiliate KTHV-TV, said two factories in an industrial park had been destroyed. Utility workers were attempting to contain a gas leak at the site.

Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd told Crowson that the county jail was no longer fit for occupancy. Eighteen inmates were being held there when the tornado struck, and all were transferred to facilities in nearby jurisdictions.

CNN invited people in the affected areas to submit photographs and video through iReport.com.

CNN’s Melissa Roberts and Dave Alsup contributed to the report.

CNN’s report concerned the tornado outbreak of April 9–10, 2009, which hit Mena, Arkansas, and Murfreesboro, Tennessee. Here is a detailed summary rather than a reproduction of CNN’s copyrighted article:

### Murfreesboro, Tennessee
- A powerful tornado swept through Murfreesboro on Good Friday, killing two people and injuring dozens.
- The victims were a mother, Kori Bryant, and her nine-week-old daughter, Olivia. The child’s father was injured.
- The storm damaged or destroyed numerous homes, overturned vehicles, uprooted trees and scattered debris through residential neighborhoods.
- Emergency crews searched damaged buildings and transported casualties to local hospitals. Officials initially cautioned that casualty and damage figures could change as searches continued.
- Rutherford County officials described a wide, destructive path through the city. The National Weather Service later rated the tornado EF4, with winds estimated in the 166–200 mph range.
- Witnesses told CNN that the sky darkened rapidly and that the tornado resembled a huge black wall. Residents described taking shelter in bathrooms, closets and interior hallways while hearing a roar and the sound of homes breaking apart.
- Murfreesboro Mayor Tommy Bragg and other local officials emphasized the extent of the residential destruction and asked people to avoid the affected neighborhoods so emergency crews could work.
- Tennessee officials declared a state of emergency and mobilized state resources, including the National Guard, to assist with searches, security and cleanup.

### Mena, Arkansas
- The tornado struck Mena the previous evening, killing three people and injuring roughly 30 others.
- It cut through the western Arkansas town, damaging homes, businesses, government buildings and utility lines. Some structures were flattened or stripped from their foundations.
- The Polk County courthouse, a hospital or medical complex, and emergency-service facilities were among the buildings reported damaged, complicating the initial response.
- Officials imposed controls on access to the damaged area because of downed power lines, debris, gas leaks and fears of additional storms.
- Local authorities described the scene as widespread devastation. Search-and-rescue teams checked collapsed buildings and homes while utility crews worked to restore electricity.
- Witnesses said the tornado arrived with little time to react. Survivors recalled taking cover as windows shattered, roofs lifted away and debris struck buildings. Some emerged to find entire blocks heavily damaged.
- Arkansas Governor Mike Beebe declared a state of emergency and traveled to the area. State police, National Guard personnel and other agencies were sent to help local responders.
- The National Weather Service subsequently classified the Mena tornado as an EF3, indicating estimated winds of 136–165 mph.

### Overall context
CNN presented the two disasters as part of the same severe-weather system moving across the South. At least five people were killed between the two cities, scores were injured, and hundreds of buildings were damaged. The report stressed that warnings and residents’ decisions to shelter likely prevented a higher death toll, while officials continued damage assessments and searches after the storms passed.
